headline: US residential proxies are a national security threat, fueling social media manipulation and spam.
summary: Residential proxies route malicious traffic through real home internet connections, making abuse appear legitimate. This makes them a critical tool for bad actors and a significant challenge for online security.
details: US residential proxies are a major source of social media manipulation and spam, routing traffic through real home internet connections. This makes malicious activity appear to originate from legitimate users on common ISPs like Comcast or AT&T.
Most users unknowingly host these proxies, often due to being tricked or hacked. Researchers found over 42% of LG smart TV apps could covertly turn TVs into proxies, leading LG to ban such apps.

Internet services struggle to block these IPs because doing so would also cut off genuine users. This unique characteristic makes US residential proxies highly valuable to bad actors for evading detection.
A 'threat intelligence' industry tracks and sells IP information, but critics argue there are perverse incentives to not fully resolve the issue, as it would diminish their market value.

The article suggests the US government, possibly the NSA, should crack down on these networks due to their national security implications. Major ISPs should also detect suspicious activity and warn customers, as proxy use negatively impacts their internet speed and can lead to IP bans.
caption:
US residential proxies are a national security threat, enabling widespread social media manipulation and spam. Many users unknowingly host these networks on their home connections.

US residential proxies are a major source of social media manipulation and spam, routing traffic through real home internet connections. This makes malicious activity appear to originate from legitimate users on common ISPs like Comcast or AT&T.

Most users unknowingly host these proxies, often due to being tricked or hacked. Researchers found over 42% of LG smart TV apps could covertly turn TVs into proxies, leading LG to ban such apps.

Internet services struggle to block these IPs because doing so would also cut off genuine users. This unique characteristic makes US residential proxies highly valuable to bad actors for evading detection.

A 'threat intelligence' industry tracks and sells IP information, but critics argue there are perverse incentives to not fully resolve the issue, as it would diminish their market value.

The article suggests the US government, possibly the NSA, should crack down on these networks due to their national security implications. Major ISPs should also detect suspicious activity and warn customers, as proxy use negatively impacts their internet speed and can lead to IP bans.
